source: Had you followed Captain Ahab down into his cabin after the squall that took place on the night succeeding that wild ratification of his purpose with his crew, you would have seen him go to a locker in the transom, and bringing out a large wrinkled roll of yellowish sea charts, spread them before him on his screwed-down table. Then seating himself before it, you would have seen him intently study the various lines and shadings which there met his eye; and with slow but steady pencil trace additional courses over spaces that before were blank. At intervals, he would refer to piles of old log-books beside him, wherein were set down the seasons and places in which, on various former voyages of various ships, sperm whales had been captured or seen.

While thus employed, the heavy pewter lamp suspended in chains over his head, continually rocked with the motion of the ship, and for ever threw shifting gleams and shadows of lines upon his wrinkled brow, till it almost seemed that while he himself was marking out lines and courses on the wrinkled charts, some invisible pencil was also tracing lines and courses upon the deeply marked chart of his forehead.

But it was not this night in particular that, in the solitude of his cabin, Ahab thus pondered over his charts. Almost every night they were brought out; almost every night some pencil marks were effaced, and others were substituted. For with the charts of all four oceans before him, Ahab was threading a maze of currents and eddies, with a view to the more certain accomplishment of that monomaniac thought of his soul.

Now, to any one not fully acquainted with the ways of the leviathans, it might seem an absurdly hopeless task thus to seek out one solitary creature in the unhooped oceans of this planet. But not so did it seem to Ahab, who knew the sets of all tides and currents; and thereby calculating the driftings of the sperm whale’s food; and, also, calling to mind the regular, ascertained seasons for hunting him in particular latitudes; could arrive at reasonable surmises, almost approaching to certainties, concerning the timeliest day to be upon this or that ground in search of his prey.

So assured, indeed, is the fact concerning the periodicalness of the sperm whale’s resorting to given waters, that many hunters believe that, could he be closely observed and studied throughout the world; were the logs for one voyage of the entire whale fleet carefully collated, then the migrations of the sperm whale would be found to correspond in invariability to those of the herring-shoals or the flights of swallows. On this hint, attempts have been made to construct elaborate migratory charts of the sperm whale.*

*Since the above was written, the statement is happily borne out by an official circular, issued by Lieutenant Maury, of the National Observatory, Washington, April 16th, 1851. By that circular, it appears that precisely such a chart is in course of completion; and portions of it are presented in the circular. “This chart divides the ocean into districts of five degrees of latitude by five degrees of longitude; perpendicularly through each of which districts are twelve columns for the twelve months; and horizontally through each of which districts are three lines; one to show the number of days that have been spent in each month in every district, and the two others to show the number of days in which whales, sperm or right, have been seen.”

Besides, when making a passage from one feeding-ground to another, the sperm whales, guided by some infallible instinct—say, rather, secret intelligence from the Deity—mostly swim in veins, as they are called; continuing their way along a given ocean-line with such undeviating exactitude, that no ship ever sailed her course, by any chart, with one tithe of such marvellous precision. Though, in these cases, the direction taken by any one whale be straight as a surveyor’s parallel, and though the line of advance be strictly confined to its own unavoidable, straight wake, yet the arbitrary vein in which at these times he is said to swim, generally embraces some few miles in width (more or less, as the vein is presumed to expand or contract); but never exceeds the visual sweep from the whale-ship’s mast-heads, when circumspectly gliding along this magic zone. The sum is, that at particular seasons within that breadth and along that path, migrating whales may with great confidence be looked for.

And hence not only at substantiated times, upon well known separate feeding-grounds, could Ahab hope to encounter his prey; but in crossing the widest expanses of water between those grounds he could, by his art, so place and time himself on his way, as even then not to be wholly without prospect of a meeting.

There was a circumstance which at first sight seemed to entangle his delirious but still methodical scheme. But not so in the reality, perhaps. Though the gregarious sperm whales have their regular seasons for particular grounds, yet in general you cannot conclude that the herds which haunted such and such a latitude or longitude this year, say, will turn out to be identically the same with those that were found there the preceding season; though there are peculiar and unquestionable instances where the contrary of this has proved true. In general, the same remark, only within a less wide limit, applies to the solitaries and hermits among the matured, aged sperm whales. So that though Moby Dick had in a former year been seen, for example, on what is called the Seychelle ground in the Indian ocean, or Volcano Bay on the Japanese Coast; yet it did not follow, that were the Pequod to visit either of those spots at any subsequent corresponding season, she would infallibly encounter him there. So, too, with some other feeding grounds, where he had at times revealed himself. But all these seemed only his casual stopping-places and ocean-inns, so to speak, not his places of prolonged abode. And where Ahab’s chances of accomplishing his object have hitherto been spoken of, allusion has only been made to whatever way-side, antecedent, extra prospects were his, ere a particular set time or place were attained, when all possibilities would become probabilities, and, as Ahab fondly thought, every possibility the next thing to a certainty. That particular set time and place were conjoined in the one technical phrase—the Season-on-the-Line. For there and then, for several consecutive years, Moby Dick had been periodically descried, lingering in those waters for awhile, as the sun, in its annual round, loiters for a predicted interval in any one sign of the Zodiac. There it was, too, that most of the deadly encounters with the white whale had taken place; there the waves were storied with his deeds; there also was that tragic spot where the monomaniac old man had found the awful motive to his vengeance. But in the cautious comprehensiveness and unloitering vigilance with which Ahab threw his brooding soul into this unfaltering hunt, he would not permit himself to rest all his hopes upon the one crowning fact above mentioned, however flattering it might be to those hopes; nor in the sleeplessness of his vow could he so tranquillize his unquiet heart as to postpone all intervening quest.

Now, the Pequod had sailed from Nantucket at the very beginning of the Season-on-the-Line. No possible endeavor then could enable her commander to make the great passage southwards, double Cape Horn, and then running down sixty degrees of latitude arrive in the equatorial Pacific in time to cruise there. Therefore, he must wait for the next ensuing season. Yet the premature hour of the Pequod’s sailing had, perhaps, been correctly selected by Ahab, with a view to this very complexion of things. Because, an interval of three hundred and sixty-five days and nights was before him; an interval which, instead of impatiently enduring ashore, he would spend in a miscellaneous hunt; if by chance the White Whale, spending his vacation in seas far remote from his periodical feeding-grounds, should turn up his wrinkled brow off the Persian Gulf, or in the Bengal Bay, or China Seas, or in any other waters haunted by his race. So that Monsoons, Pampas, Nor’-Westers, Harmattans, Trades; any wind but the Levanter and Simoon, might blow Moby Dick into the devious zig-zag world-circle of the Pequod’s circumnavigating wake.

But granting all this; yet, regarded discreetly and coolly, seems it not but a mad idea, this; that in the broad boundless ocean, one solitary whale, even if encountered, should be thought capable of individual recognition from his hunter, even as a white-bearded Mufti in the thronged thoroughfares of Constantinople? Yes. For the peculiar snow-white brow of Moby Dick, and his snow-white hump, could not but be unmistakable. And have I not tallied the whale, Ahab would mutter to himself, as after poring over his charts till long after midnight he would throw himself back in reveries—tallied him, and shall he escape? His broad fins are bored, and scalloped out like a lost sheep’s ear! And here, his mad mind would run on in a breathless race; till a weariness and faintness of pondering came over him; and in the open air of the deck he would seek to recover his strength. Ah, God! what trances of torments does that man endure who is consumed with one unachieved revengeful desire. He sleeps with clenched hands; and wakes with his own bloody nails in his palms.

Often, when forced from his hammock by exhausting and intolerably vivid dreams of the night, which, resuming his own intense thoughts through the day, carried them on amid a clashing of phrensies, and whirled them round and round and round in his blazing brain, till the very throbbing of his life-spot became insufferable anguish; and when, as was sometimes the case, these spiritual throes in him heaved his being up from its base, and a chasm seemed opening in him, from which forked flames and lightnings shot up, and accursed fiends beckoned him to leap down among them; when this hell in himself yawned beneath him, a wild cry would be heard through the ship; and with glaring eyes Ahab would burst from his state room, as though escaping from a bed that was on fire. Yet these, perhaps, instead of being the unsuppressable symptoms of some latent weakness, or fright at his own resolve, were but the plainest tokens of its intensity. For, at such times, crazy Ahab, the scheming, unappeasedly steadfast hunter of the white whale; this Ahab that had gone to his hammock, was not the agent that so caused him to burst from it in horror again. The latter was the eternal, living principle or soul in him; and in sleep, being for the time dissociated from the characterizing mind, which at other times employed it for its outer vehicle or agent, it spontaneously sought escape from the scorching contiguity of the frantic thing, of which, for the time, it was no longer an integral. But as the mind does not exist unless leagued with the soul, therefore it must have been that, in Ahab’s case, yielding up all his thoughts and fancies to his one supreme purpose; that purpose, by its own sheer inveteracy of will, forced itself against gods and devils into a kind of self-assumed, independent being of its own. Nay, could grimly live and burn, while the common vitality to which it was conjoined, fled horror-stricken from the unbidden and unfathered birth. Therefore, the tormented spirit that glared out of bodily eyes, when what seemed Ahab rushed from his room, was for the time but a vacated thing, a formless somnambulistic being, a ray of living light, to be sure, but without an object to colour, and therefore a blankness in itself. God help thee, old man, thy thoughts have created a creature in thee; and he whose intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus; a vulture feeds upon that heart for ever; that vulture the very creature he creates.

Indeed, it could grimly live and burn while the common vitality to which it was joined fled horror-stricken from the unbidden and unfathered birth. Therefore the tormented spirit that glared out of bodily eyes, when what seemed Ahab rushed from his room, was for the time only an emptied thing, a formless sleepwalking being — a ray of living light, to be sure, but without an object to color, and therefore a blankness in itself. God help you, old man, your thoughts have created a creature in you; and he whose intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus — a vulture feeds upon that heart forever; that vulture the very creature he creates.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 44 — Søkortet
paragraphs: Hvis du var fulgt efter kaptajn Ahab ned i hans kahyt efter den byge, der kom natten efter den vilde stadfæstelse af hans formål over for mandskabet, ville du have set ham gå hen til et skab agter, tage en stor, krøllet rulle gullige søkort frem og brede dem ud foran sig på det fastboltede bord. Så, siddende foran dem, ville du have set ham studere de forskellige linjer og skraveringer, der mødte hans øje, med nøje opmærksomhed, og med langsom men fast blyant tegne nye kurser hen over områder, der før havde været tomme. Med mellemrum slog han op i stakkene af gamle logbøger ved siden af sig, hvori det stod skrevet, i hvilke årstider og på hvilke steder kaskelotter var blevet fanget eller set på forskellige tidligere rejser med forskellige skibe.

Mens han arbejdede sådan, gyngede den tunge tinlampe, der hang i kæder over ham, uafbrudt med skibets bevægelse og kastede skiftende glimt og skygger af linjer hen over hans furede pande. Det var næsten, som om der, mens han selv afsatte linjer og kurser på de krøllede søkort, også var en usynlig blyant, der tegnede linjer og kurser på hans dybt furede panses søkort.

Men det var ikke kun denne ene nat, at Ahab grundede over sine søkort alene i sin kahyt. Næsten hver nat blev de taget frem. Næsten hver nat blev nogle blyantstreger visket ud og andre sat i stedet. For med kortene over alle fire verdenshave bredt ud foran sig fandt Ahab vej gennem et virvar af strømme og hvirvler, alt sammen for at nå sin sjæls monomane tanke med større sikkerhed.

Nu kunne det for enhver, der ikke kender leviatanernes færden til bunds, se ud som en håbløs og tåbelig opgave at opsøge ét eneste dyr i planetens grænseløse have. Men ikke for Ahab. Han kendte alle tidevandets og strømmenes mønstre. Ved at regne på, hvordan kaskelottens føde driver rundt, og ved at huske de faste, velkendte årstider for jagten på ham i bestemte breddegrader kunne han nå frem til rimelige skøn, der næsten var sikre, om den mest belejlige dag til at være på dette eller hint fangstfelt for at finde sit bytte.

Kaskelottens tilbagevenden til bestemte farvande med jævne mellemrum er faktisk så velkendt, at mange fangstmænd tror, at hvis man kunne iagttage og studere ham nøje over hele verden — hvis man omhyggeligt sammenlignede skibsjournalerne fra én eneste rejse for hele hvalfangerflåden — så ville kaskelottens vandringer vise sig at være lige så uforanderlige som sildestimernes eller svalernes træk. På dette fingerpeg har man forsøgt at lave omfattende vandringskort over kaskelotten.*

*Siden jeg skrev ovenstående, er påstanden glædeligt blevet bekræftet af et officielt cirkulære, udsendt af løjtnant Maury fra Det Nationale Observatorium i Washington den 16. april 1851. Cirkulæret viser, at netop sådan et kort nu er ved at blive færdiggjort, og dele af det er gengivet i cirkulæret. »Dette kort deler havet op i distrikter på fem breddegrader gange fem længdegrader. Lodret gennem hvert af disse distrikter går der tolv kolonner for årets tolv måneder, og vandret gennem hvert distrikt går der tre linjer: én, der viser, hvor mange dage der er blevet tilbragt i hvert distrikt i hver måned, og to andre, der viser, på hvor mange dage der er set hvaler, kaskelotter eller rethvaler.«

Desuden svømmer kaskelotterne, når de skal fra ét fødeområde til et andet, mest i det, man kalder årer. De er styret af et ufejlbarligt instinkt, eller rettere, lad os sige, af hemmelig besked fra Gud selv. De følger en bestemt linje gennem havet så nøjagtigt og uden at vige, at intet skib nogen sinde har sejlet sin kurs efter noget kort med en tiendedel af den forbløffende præcision. I sådanne tilfælde kan retningen, en enkelt hval tager, være lige som en landmålers parallel, og hans fremfærd kan være strengt begrænset til hans eget uundgåelige, snorlige kølvand. Alligevel dækker den vilkårlige åre, han siges at svømme i på de tidspunkter, som regel en bredde på nogle få engelske mil (mere eller mindre, eftersom åren menes at udvide sig eller trække sig sammen), men aldrig mere, end øjet kan række fra hvalfangerens mastetoppe, mens hun forsigtigt glider langs denne trylleagtige zone. Resultatet er, at man på bestemte årstider kan vente at finde vandrende hvaler inden for den bredde og langs den vej med stor sikkerhed.

Og så kunne Ahab ikke kun håbe at møde sit bytte på bestemte tider, på de velkendte, adskilte fødeområder. Selv når han krydsede de allerbredeste strækninger af vand mellem disse områder, kunne han med sin dygtighed placere og time sig undervejs, så der stadig var udsigt til et møde.

Der var en omstændighed, som ved første øjekast syntes at forvirre hans vanvittige, men stadig metodiske plan. Men måske gjorde den det i virkeligheden ikke. De flokdannende kaskelotter har nok deres faste årstider på bestemte fangstfelter, men man kan som regel ikke slutte, at de flokke, der holdt til i den og den bredde- eller længdegrad i år, for eksempel, vil vise sig at være nøjagtig de samme, som man fandt der sæsonen før — selv om der findes besynderlige og ubestridelige tilfælde, hvor det modsatte har vist sig at være rigtigt. Generelt gælder den samme bemærkning, blot inden for snævrere grænser, for de ensomme og eneboerne blandt de fuldvoksne, gamle kaskelotter. Så selv om Moby Dick i et tidligere år var set, for eksempel, på det, man kalder Seychelle-feltet i Det Indiske Ocean eller i Volcano Bay ved den japanske kyst, fulgte det ikke, at hvis Pequod besøgte et af de steder på en senere tilsvarende årstid, ville hun uundgåeligt møde ham der. Det samme gjaldt nogle andre fødeområder, hvor han til tider havde vist sig. Men alle disse syntes kun at være hans tilfældige hvilesteder og havets værtshuse, om man så må sige, ikke steder, hvor han boede længe. Og når Ahabs chancer for at nå sit mål hidtil har været omtalt, er der kun tænkt på de tilfældige, forberedende ekstra muligheder, han havde, før et bestemt fastsat tidspunkt eller sted var nået — hvor alle muligheder ville blive til sandsynligheder, og hvor enhver mulighed, som Ahab naivt troede, ville være så godt som en vished. Det bestemte tidspunkt og sted var samlet i ét fagudtryk: Sæsonen-ved-Linjen (Linjen er ækvator). For netop dér og da var Moby Dick i flere år i træk med jævne mellemrum set, mens han opholdt sig en tid i de farvande, ligesom solen på sin årlige rundtur dvæler et forudsagt stykke tid i hvert enkelt tegn i Dyrekredsen. Det var også dér, de fleste af de dødelige sammenstød med den hvide hval havde fundet sted. Dér var selve bølgerne fulde af beretninger om hans gerninger, og dér lå også det tragiske sted, hvor den monomane gamle mand havde fundet det frygtelige motiv til sin hævn. Men Ahab kastede sin grublende sjæl ind i denne urokkelige jagt med så forsigtig grundighed og så rastløs årvågenhed, at han ikke ville lade sig nøjes med at lægge alle sine forhåbninger på det ene afgørende forhold, der netop er nævnt, hvor smigrende det end var for dem. Og i sit løftes søvnløshed kunne han heller ikke berolige sit urolige hjerte så meget, at han opgav al søgen i mellemtiden.

Nu var Pequod sejlet fra Nantucket lige i begyndelsen af Sæsonen-ved-Linjen. Ingen mulig anstrengelse kunne have sat hendes kaptajn i stand til at gennemføre den lange sejlads sydpå rundt om Kap Horn og derefter, ved at løbe tres breddegrader ned, nå frem til det ækvatoriale Stillehav i tide til at krydse dér. Derfor måtte han vente til næste sæson. Alligevel var tidspunktet for Pequods tidlige afsejling måske rigtigt valgt af Ahab med netop denne situation for øje. For der lå et tidsrum på trehundrede og femogtres dage og nætter foran ham — et tidsrum, som han i stedet for at udholde det utålmodigt i land ville bruge på en blandet jagt, for det tilfælde at den hvide hval, der holdt ferie i have langt fra sine faste fødeområder, ved et tilfælde skulle vise sin rynkede pande ud for Den Persiske Bugt eller i Den Bengalske Bugt eller i Det Kinesiske Hav eller i andre farvande, hvor hans slægt holder til. Så monsuner, pampero'er, nordvestlige storme, harmattaner, passatvinde — enhver vind undtagen levanten og simumen — kunne blæse Moby Dick ind i den bugtede zigzagrundtur, som Pequods kølvand beskrev rundt om verden.

Men når man indrømmer alt dette og ser nøgternt og koldt på det, ser det så ikke ud som en gal idé — at én enkelt hval i det brede, grænseløse hav, selv om man støder på den, skulle antages at kunne genkendes personligt af sin jæger, som en hvidskægget mufti i Konstantinopels myldrende gader? Jo. For Moby Dicks særprægede snehvide pande og hans snehvide pukkel kunne ikke undgå at være umiskendelige. Og har jeg ikke talt hvalens mærker op, mumlede Ahab for sig selv, når han efter at have stirret på sine kort til længe efter midnat lod sig falde tilbage i drømmerier — talt ham op, og skulle han så slippe væk? Hans brede finner er gennemboret og udhulet i kanten som et fortabt fårs øre! Og her løb hans gale sind videre i et åndeløst væddeløb, indtil en træthed og svimmelhed efter al grublerien kom over ham, og han søgte at hente kræfter igen i den åbne luft på dækket. Ak, Gud! Hvilke pinsler af trance den mand lider, som fortæres af ét uopfyldt hævnønske. Han sover med knyttede hænder og vågner med sine egne blodige negle i håndfladerne.

Ofte, når han blev drevet ud af sin hængekøje af nattens udmattende og uudholdeligt levende drømme — drømme, som tog hans egne intense tanker fra dagen og førte dem videre midt i et sammenstød af vanvid og hvirvlede dem rundt og rundt og rundt i hans glødende hjerne, indtil selve hans livspunkts banken blev en ulidelig kval — og når disse åndelige veer, som det af og til skete, løftede hele hans væsen op fra grunden, og det var, som om en kløft åbnede sig i ham, hvorfra gaflede flammer og lyn skød op, og forbandede djævle vinkede ham til at springe ned mellem dem — når dette helvede inde i ham gabede under ham, hørtes et vildt skrig gennem skibet, og med stirrende øjne brød Ahab ud af sin kahyt, som om han slap væk fra en seng, der stod i brand. Men disse udbrud var måske, i stedet for at være ukontrollerbare symptomer på en skjult svaghed eller på skræk for hans eget forsæt, kun de tydeligste tegn på dets styrke. For på sådanne tidspunkter var den gale Ahab, den planlæggende, ustandseligt stædige jæger af den hvide hval — den Ahab, som var gået i sin hængekøje — ikke den kraft, der fik ham til at bryde ud af den igen i rædsel. Den kraft var det evige, levende princip, eller sjælen, i ham. I søvne, hvor den for en tid var skilt fra det karakteriserende sind, som ellers brugte den som sit ydre redskab eller sin ydre agent, søgte den af sig selv at flygte fra den brændende nærhed af den vanvittige ting, som den for en tid ikke længere var en del af. Men da sindet ikke eksisterer, medmindre det er forbundet med sjælen, må det have været sådan, at i Ahabs tilfælde, mens han overgav alle sine tanker og indfald til sit ene højeste formål, tvang dette formål sig, ved sin egen viljes rene stædighed, mod guder og djævle, ind i en slags selvtaget, uafhængig væren for sig selv. Ja, det kunne grumt leve og brænde, mens den almindelige livskraft, det var forbundet med, flygtede rædselsslagen fra den uindbudte og faderløse fødsel. Derfor var den pinte ånd, der glimtede ud af kropslige øjne, da det, der så ud til at være Ahab, styrtede ud af sit rum, for en tid kun en tømt ting, et formløst, søvngængeragtigt væsen — en stråle levende lys, ganske vist, men uden noget at farve og derfor selv et tomrum. Gud hjælpe dig, gamle mand, dine tanker har skabt et væsen i dig. Og den, hvis intense tænkning således gør ham til en Prometheus — en grib æder af det hjerte for evigt, og den grib er selve det væsen, han skaber.
